newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Fiscal lenience needed for African oil investment.
newsitem.headline: Fiscal lenience needed for African oil investment.

text.p: Friendly fiscal regimes and technological improvements should play a major role in increasing investment in oil and gas exploration and development in Africa, a conference was told on Wednesday.

The president and chairman of Mobil North Sea Ltd, John Cousins, told the Africa Upsteam '96 conference that Africa's "significant" political and technical risk would not deter investors as long as there was an understanding of risk and reward between investors and the host country.

Exxon West Africa ventures manager James Fleece also stressed the importance of attractive fiscal regimes, but said recent technological developments would play just as important a role in attracting investment.
"Several recent technological developments provide both cost and risk reduction benefits," he said.
In particular, seismic technology had experienced "tremendous advances since the 1980s" and new 3-D seismic methods allowed "higher wildcat success rates and more accurate appraisal well selection."
Well logging and drilling techniques had also been improved while innovative production methods "continue to push back the limit of what is operationally feasible."

Energy Africa Ltd managing director John Bentley said African oil output of about seven million barrels per day accounted for only 10 percent of world production, even though African output had been growing at a faster pace than in the rest of the world over the last 10 years.
He said Africa had six percent of world reserves, making it the third most important region after the Middle East and Latin America.
Libya and Nigeria dominated about two-thirds of African output and it was clear that others were producing at levels well below the capacity of their reserve base.
"It is no surprise that countries which have been the most successful in exploiting their reserves tend to be those which are the most open to investment," Bentley said.
Cousins predicted that West Africa would continue to be active in both gas and oil, with gas exports increasing to Europe and Mediterranean countries.
In Southern Africa, greater emphasis would be placed on developing gas reserves such as Mozambique's Pande and Namibia's Kudu, hopefully linked to industrial growth.
